A perpendicular line is drawn from a point $P$ on the diagonal $BD$ to intersect $AB$ at point $F$ and $CD$ at point $E$. A line is drawn through point $E$ such that $EG \parallel BD$ and intersects $BC$ at point $G$. The line $FG$ intersects $BD$ at point $H$, and $DF$ is connected. When the quadrilateral $DFGE$ has one pair of adjacent sides equal, what is the length of $BG$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:}

(1) As shown in Figure 1, when $DE=EG$, let $BG=x$, then $DE=EG=2x$, $CE=2-2x$, $CG=1-x$. In $\triangle CEG$ with a right angle, $CE^{2}+CG^{2}=EG^{2}$,
\[
\therefore (2-2x)^{2}+(1-x)^{2}=(2x)^{2},
\]
solving this yields $x=5-2\sqrt{5}$,
\[
\therefore \boxed{BG=5-2\sqrt{5}};
\]

(2) As shown in Figure 1, when $EG=GF$,
\[
\because CE=BF, \angle C=\angle ABC=90^\circ,
\]
\[
\therefore \text{Rt}\triangle ECG\cong \text{Rt}\triangle FBG \text{ (by the HL congruence theorem)},
\]
\[
\therefore \boxed{BG=CG=\frac{1}{2}CB=\frac{1}{2}},
\]

(3) As shown in Figure 1, when $DF=GF$, let $BG=x$, then $AF=DE=2x$,
\[
\because DF^{2}=GF^{2},
\]
\[
\therefore DA^{2}+AF^{2}=BG^{2}+BF^{2},
\]
\[
\therefore 1^{2}+(2x)^{2}=(2-2x)^{2}+x^{2},
\]
solving this yields $x=4\pm\sqrt{13}$,
\[
\because BG<1,
\]
\[
\therefore \boxed{BG=4-\sqrt{13}};
\]

(4) $\because \angle DEF=90^\circ$,
\[
\therefore DF>DE, \text{ i.e., } DF=DE \text{ does not exist};
\]

In summary, the length of $BG$ can be \boxed{5-2\sqrt{5}}, \boxed{\frac{1}{2}}, or \boxed{4-\sqrt{13}}.

raw_record.original_question: As shown in the figure, in rectangle $ABCD$, $BC=1$, $AB=2$. A perpendicular line is drawn from a point $P$ on the diagonal $BD$ to intersect $AB$ at point $F$ and $CD$ at point $E$. A line is drawn through point $E$ such that $EG \parallel BD$ and intersects $BC$ at point $G$. The line $FG$ intersects $BD$ at point $H$, and $DF$ is connected. When the quadrilateral $DFGE$ has one pair of adjacent sides equal, what is the length of $BG$?

\textbf{Solution:}

(1) As shown in Figure 1, when $DE=EG$, let $BG=x$, then $DE=EG=2x$, $CE=2-2x$, $CG=1-x$. In $\triangle CEG$ with a right angle, $CE^{2}+CG^{2}=EG^{2}$,
\[
\therefore (2-2x)^{2}+(1-x)^{2}=(2x)^{2},
\]
solving this yields $x=5-2\sqrt{5}$,
\[
\therefore \boxed{BG=5-2\sqrt{5}};
\]

(2) As shown in Figure 1, when $EG=GF$,
\[
\because CE=BF, \angle C=\angle ABC=90^\circ,
\]
\[
\therefore \text{Rt}\triangle ECG\cong \text{Rt}\triangle FBG \text{ (by the HL congruence theorem)},
\]
\[
\therefore \boxed{BG=CG=\frac{1}{2}CB=\frac{1}{2}},
\]

(3) As shown in Figure 1, when $DF=GF$, let $BG=x$, then $AF=DE=2x$,
\[
\because DF^{2}=GF^{2},
\]
\[
\therefore DA^{2}+AF^{2}=BG^{2}+BF^{2},
\]
\[
\therefore 1^{2}+(2x)^{2}=(2-2x)^{2}+x^{2},
\]
solving this yields $x=4\pm\sqrt{13}$,
\[
\because BG<1,
\]
\[
\therefore \boxed{BG=4-\sqrt{13}};
\]

(4) $\because \angle DEF=90^\circ$,
\[
\therefore DF>DE, \text{ i.e., } DF=DE \text{ does not exist};
\]

In summary, the length of $BG$ can be \boxed{5-2\sqrt{5}}, \boxed{\frac{1}{2}}, or \boxed{4-\sqrt{13}}
